newsitem.title: BOSNIA: OSCE names November 22-24 for local Bosnian poll.
newsitem.headline: OSCE names November 22-24 for local Bosnian poll.

text.p: Bosnian voters will go to the polls from November 22-24 to elect local councils, the senior diplomat responsible for organising them announced on Friday, ending widespread speculation about the timing of the vote.
Robert Frowick said he had made "a chairman's decision" to go ahead with the election on that date after a lengthy discussion with the Provisional Election Commission.

Frowick heads the Bosnian mission of the Organisation for Cooperation and Security in Europe (OSCE), which postponed the municipal elections after discovering irregularities in registering Serb refugees.

The municipal poll was to have taken place alongside the September 14 vote for a presidency and national and regional assemblies, which was designed to reunite the country under jointly elected institutions.
Independent election observers have criticised the widely anticipated November date as too early to address the irregularities.
According to the OSCE, Serb authorities used refugees to stack the electoral odds in key municipalities now under their control, but which had pre-war Moslem or Croat majorities.

In his statement, Frowick acknowledged it was a difficult decision that had the support of all three ethnic groups, but was opposed by one of three international members of the Provisional Election Commission -- the top organising body.
"The decision...was taken in full knowledge that we will be engaged in a high-risk operational program," Frowick told a news conference.
"There is very little time to restore personnel requirements at full strength, ensure higher standards than prevailed on the six levels of elections on 14 September, funding and so on."
But the U.S. diplomat also insisted he had the support of the international community -- the key prerequisite for a successfull poll.

"My principle reason for staying on track with municipal elections before the end of the year is to take full advantage of the strength of the international community's presence, in both its civil and military dimensions, before that presence is significantly diminished in 1997," he said.
The municipal elections are the most politicaly sensitive of Bosnia's votes.

Under the electoral rules, people are allowed to vote in municipalities where they lived before the war. In theory that could mean some towns that were ethnicaly cleansed during the war could end up with mayors who are unable to travel there.

The poll is also likely to present bigger security headaches than September's election. Thousands of people wishing to vote in towns they were forced to abandon may have to cross old front lines into rival territory to do so.
To complicate matters further, at least five senior OSCE officials have left their posts, taking valuable experience with them.
The OSCE said they had either resigned or decided not to extend their contracts, amid speculation they were leaving because of dissatisfaction over the running of the elections.

"Changing the team at this stage is a very poor omen for municipal elections and makes it unlikely they will go smoothly," said Chris Bennett, a spokesman for the International Crisis Group (ICG) which is monitoring the peace process.
